Feed directory

1300 data feeds across 40 categories. This is the list of sources Trooth intends to route to, with the reason each one is on it. It is not a list of sources you can call today: 5 of them are merged into the routing catalog, and the rest are candidates.

A feed becomes routable only after somebody reads its terms from the source's own documentation and cites the URL, alongside declarative adapter fields and a live fetch in CI. Until that happens it is listed here and nowhere else, it never appears in an envelope, and it carries no grade, because nothing about it has been measured.

What the categories are for

The grouping is not decorative. Each category was chosen because it exercises something the others do not: feeds that revise for weeks after publication, feeds that correct in seconds, feeds with a settled result at the end that a forecast can honestly be scored against.

agriculture commodities · 20

Crop and livestock statistics, physical commodity prices, and trade flows. The interesting property of this group is the estimate-then-settle pattern: a production forecast is issued monthly, revised monthly, and eventually replaced by a survey. That is a correction-latency dimension with a real anchor at the end of it, which few other domains offer.

agriculture trade · 35

Agricultural reporting, food prices, and trade statistics. What distinguishes this group is that the release instant has direct monetary value, so the gap between publication and availability is not an abstraction. It is also full of mirror publishing: the same crop estimate appears in a national release, an international database, and a market newsletter, each with a different vintage and none citing the others. Candidates only, terms unread.

aviation maritime · 40

Aviation and maritime movement data, plus the regulators that publish the reference data behind it. Two things make this group unusual. The positional feeds are crowd-sourced as often as they are official, so the primary is frequently a volunteer network rather than an authority; and the commercial terms are strict enough that several entries here will never be promotable under H3. Recording that is the point. Candidates only, terms unread.

central banks · 35

Central banks and monetary authorities. These are the cleanest primaries in the registry: a policy rate has one publisher, the publication instant is recorded to the minute, and every aggregator downstream is provably a derivative. That makes the group the best available test bed for freshness lag and for lineage inference. Candidates only, terms unread.

civic transparency · 20

Sanctions lists, procurement, lobbying, campaign finance, and political event data. Sanctions lists are the one group in the registry where staleness is a compliance failure rather than an inconvenience, which makes freshness lag the dimension that matters most and the one a caller would actually pay to have measured. Most of the rest is derivative of filings that are already elsewhere in the registry, which makes the group a good lineage exhibit.

courts legal · 35

Courts, legislation, and legal publishers beyond the entries already registered. Legal data has a property the rest of the registry mostly lacks: the authoritative version is a specific document at a specific moment, and citing the wrong vintage is not a quality issue but an error. That makes as_of replay less of a feature and more of a requirement. Candidates only, terms unread.

crypto markets · 30

Blockchain nodes, indexers, and crypto market data. This group is worth registering for one reason that has nothing to do with crypto as an asset class: it is the only domain where the underlying record is already content-addressed and independently verifiable, so a disagreement between two providers about the same block is unambiguously one provider being wrong. That is the cleanest accuracy anchor available to us anywhere. Candidates only, terms unread.

culture media sports · 20

Cultural heritage collections, media metadata, and sports results. The heritage half is slow, open, and heavily attributed, which exercises the attribution string in license_chain more than any other group. The sports half is the opposite: seconds matter, corrections are common during a game, and the settled result at the end is a genuine anchor. Phase 4 names graded sports feeds as a vertical, so these entries are targets rather than hypotheses.

cyber internet · 39

Vulnerability catalogues, threat intelligence, and internet measurement. This group is the one where an agent is most likely to act on a tool result immediately, which makes two of our rules load-bearing at once: advisory text is attacker-controllable and belongs in untrusted_text (H5), and a vulnerability record that has been superseded is worse than no record at all. Candidates only, terms unread.

earth observation · 40

Satellite and remote sensing archives, and the derived products built on them. Two properties make this group different from the rest of the registry. Products are reprocessed in numbered collections, so the same observation legitimately has several values and the collection is part of the answer; and volumes are large enough that fetching without caching is a cost decision rather than a performance one. Candidates only, terms unread.

elections parliaments · 40

Election authorities, parliamentary records, and legislative data. Election night is the single hardest freshness problem in public data: results are provisional for hours, corrected for weeks, certified once, and republished by dozens of derivatives that rarely say which vintage they hold. Parliamentary records are the opposite, slow and append-only, which makes the pair useful together. Candidates only, terms unread.

energy climate · 20

Electricity markets, grid operators, and emissions accounting. Grid operators publish on a five-minute clock and then revise settlement data for weeks, which makes this the group with the sharpest revision behaviour and correction latency signals in the registry. Emissions inventories sit at the other end: annual, heavily restated, and mostly derivative.

energy grids · 46

Grid operators, system operators, and energy regulators. Electricity data has a property almost nothing else in this registry has: the same quantity is published three times, first as a forecast, then as a near-realtime estimate, then as a settled figure weeks later, each by the same publisher. That makes revision behaviour and correction latency measurable without any external anchor, which is why the group is worth this much of the registry. Candidates only.

environment hazards · 20

Disasters, hazards, and environmental monitoring. An alert feed is the one place where every dimension we measure has an obvious cost attached: late is dangerous, wrong is worse, and a silent revision after the fact is how people stop trusting a source. Several entries here duplicate each other deliberately, because two agencies reporting the same earthquake with different magnitudes is the clearest possible demonstration of what compare is for.

finance markets · 20

Central banks, international statistical agencies, market data, and crypto. Financial data is where redistribution terms bite hardest: several widely used endpoints are free to call and still forbid republication, which is exactly the distinction the licence chain exists to carry. Nothing here is promoted without reading the terms in full.

financial regulators · 40

Securities regulators, prudential supervisors, and the disclosure systems they run. Filings are the ideal shape for a provenance envelope: each one has an accession identifier, a filing timestamp, an amendment chain, and a legal consequence for being wrong. The interesting scoring question here is not freshness but correction latency, since an amended filing supersedes an original that many downstreams never revisit. Candidates only, terms unread.

geo transport · 20

Geography, mapping, aviation, marine, transit, and earth observation. This group has the tightest freshness requirements in the catalog, measured in seconds rather than hours, and it contains several sources whose terms restrict commercial use or redistribution, so the licence reading here matters more than anywhere else.

government · 20

United States federal statistical, regulatory, and fiscal feeds. Most works of the US federal government are public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105, but that is a rule about authorship and not a substitute for reading a given agency's own terms, so every entry here still starts at license_status unverified. Five entries are promoted because their terms were read and cited during Phase 0.

health agencies · 45

Public health agencies, medicines regulators, and disease surveillance systems. This group has the highest cost of a stale or wrong answer in the whole registry, and the worst revision discipline: case counts are backfilled for weeks, definitions change mid-series, and agencies routinely republish each other without saying so. It is the strongest argument for the envelope. Candidates only, terms unread.

internet infrastructure · 20

Routing, addressing, naming, measurement, and abuse data. Several of these are the closest public analogue to what Trooth does, in that they are measurement platforms that publish both a reading and the vantage point it was taken from. That makes them useful as prior art as well as as sources. It is also the group with the highest density of terms that forbid redistribution outright, which is worth learning early rather than late.

labor demographics · 20

Population, labour, migration, and education statistics. Almost everything here is a survey, which means published confidence intervals, suppressed cells in small geographies, and scheduled restatements. That makes the group the best available test of completeness by segment: a national total that looks fine while half the sub-geographies are blank.

legal ip · 20

Court records, legislation, patents, and trademarks. Two things make this group distinctive. Documents are append-only by nature, which suits an archive, and several of the richest sources charge per page or per seat, which puts the licence question first rather than last. Nothing here is routable until the terms are read, and several entries exist to record a no.

natstats africa mideast · 30

Statistical offices across Africa and the Middle East. Coverage here is thinner and more intermittent than in Europe, and that is the point: a scorecard that reports a real publication gap is more honest than an aggregator that interpolates over it. Candidates only, terms unread.

natstats americas · 30

Statistical institutes and regional aggregators across the Americas. The interesting property of this group is disagreement: several of these economies have had their official inflation or GDP series publicly contested, and a router that reports what two sources say without ranking them is more useful here than anywhere else. All entries are candidates with unread terms.

natstats asia pacific · 30

Statistical offices across Asia and the Pacific. This is the group where the gap between a national primary and its international republisher is widest, both in time and in definition, so it is where `trooth.compare` has the most to say. Candidates only; no terms have been read.

natstats europe · 30

National statistical institutes across Europe. Eurostat already aggregates most of what these publish, which is exactly why they matter to a router: the national office is the primary and Eurostat is the derivative, so the pair is a ready-made lineage test with a measurable publication gap between them. Every entry here is a candidate and no terms have been read.

opendata portals intl · 46

National and supranational open data catalogues outside the United States. A portal is not a source, it is an index of sources, and treating it as one is a mistake worth naming here: the value is that most of these carry per-dataset licence metadata, which is the cheapest way to find candidates that could clear rule H3 at all. Candidates only, terms unread.

opendata us cities · 51

Municipal open data portals. City data is the part of the public record that changes hourly rather than quarterly, so it is where freshness lag, silent revision, and schema drift are all observable within a single working day. It is also where licence terms are least often stated, which makes it a good stress test for rule H3. Candidates only, terms unread.

opendata us states · 52

State-level open data portals in the United States. Most run on a handful of platforms, which is the reason to register them together: one declarative adapter per platform covers dozens of publishers, and the differences that remain are exactly the ones worth scoring. Several states have no central portal and appear here without a homepage until someone confirms one. All entries are candidates and none has had its terms read.

reference security · 20

Encyclopaedic and reference corpora, plus security advisory feeds. The reference sources are where schema drift and revision behaviour are most extreme, which makes them good stress tests. The security feeds are the clearest case of correction latency mattering to somebody: a CVE amended a week late is a week of wrong answers.

registries procurement · 40

Company registries, beneficial ownership records, public procurement, and aid and spending transparency. These are the feeds that answer "who is this counterparty and what have they been paid", which is the question the demand register returns to most often. They are also the group where redistribution terms are most restrictive, because several registries fund themselves by selling the very data they publish. Candidates only, terms unread.

science archives · 45

Research repositories, bibliographic databases, and discipline archives. Science solved parts of the provenance problem long before anyone marketed it: a DOI is a content identifier, a data release is versioned, and a retraction is a published correction with a date. The value here is partly the data and partly the prior art. Candidates only, terms unread.

science health · 20

Biomedical, scholarly, environmental, and public health feeds. This group carries the regulatory wedge (openFDA and friends) and the sources with the most interesting revision and completeness behaviour, because science corrects itself in public and on a schedule.

software ecosystem · 20

Package registries and the services that index them. This group is the closest thing the registry has to a control group: releases are immutable once published, timestamps are exact, and cadence is high, so a freshness number here is unusually clean. It is also where lineage is obvious, since every aggregator names the registries it mirrors and lags them by hours.

space astronomy · 20

Orbital elements, planetary ephemerides, and astronomical archives. Astronomy solved provenance before anyone called it that: catalogs carry bibcodes, data releases are numbered, and alerts carry the instrument and the exposure that produced them. That makes this group less a source of customers than a source of prior art, plus a few feeds that decay fast enough to make freshness lag obvious. Orbital elements are stale within days, and everyone knows it.

sports culture · 40

Sports results and cultural heritage collections. They sit together because they are the two domains where the audience notices a stale answer instantly and where the licence position is least like the rest of the registry: sports data is aggressively commercial and heritage data is aggressively open. Routing correctly between them exercises the use-class machinery from both ends. Candidates only, terms unread.

transit gtfs us · 51

United States transit agencies publishing GTFS schedules and, in most cases, GTFS-Realtime. This is the single best-shaped group in the registry: one specification, hundreds of independent publishers, and a realtime feed whose staleness is both measurable and consequential to a rider. If freshness lag cannot be scored here it cannot be scored anywhere. The static and realtime halves of an agency are one entry; the adapter distinguishes them. Candidates only.

transit intl · 45

Transit and mobility publishers outside the United States, including national aggregators that republish dozens of operators under one licence. The aggregators matter more than any single operator here: they are derivatives with a stated refresh interval, so the gap between an operator's own publication and the aggregator's copy is a lineage measurement we can take without any privileged access. Candidates only, terms unread.

water environment · 40

Hydrology, water quality, and environmental monitoring networks. Gauge networks are the purest freshness problem in the registry: a station either reported in the last interval or it did not, there is no interpretation involved, and the failure mode during a flood is exactly when the data matters most. Several of these are also provisional-then-approved publishers, which gives revision behaviour a clean definition. Candidates only, terms unread.

weather services · 45

National meteorological services and the model outputs they publish. Weather is the domain where a freshness claim is easiest to falsify: a forecast has a run time, an issue time, and a valid time, all three stated in the product itself, so lag is arithmetic rather than interpretation. It is also the domain with the widest spread of licences, from public domain to strictly commercial, which makes it a good proving ground for use-class routing. Candidates only.

Showing all 1300 feeds.

The terms column is a guess, recorded to decide which terms pages to read first. It has not been verified against anything and it is not a statement about what you may do with a feed. Read the source's own terms before you rely on it.

The benchmark column is not ours. Every cell in it is fetched from Modafied when you load this page, so it shows whatever the benchmark currently publishes rather than whatever we last copied down. Most rows read not benchmarked, which means Modafied has no measurement of that feed — a fact about the benchmark's coverage, not a verdict on the data. A graded cell carries a trace id that resolves to the scorecard and method version behind it, and it can fall without notice, including for feeds we route to and pay to have measured.

Why five and not three hundred

Verifying 1300 licences by reading 1300 terms pages is real work that cannot be faked, and a catalog of 1300 entries carrying invented licence confirmations would destroy the only thing this project has to sell. So the registry states the intent and the catalog states the fact, and the gap between them is visible on this page rather than hidden behind a number.

The 5 blocked entries are the useful half of that discipline. Each one names what the obstacle is, so nobody researches the same licence twice and nobody quietly routes to it anyway. 24 feeds are marked priority one, which means a customer asked or the feed demonstrates something no other entry covers.
